body_markdown:
Great cars can occasionally take time to make their presence known. Sure, there are immediate hits that become cultural icons from day one, but most of the cars that have made the strongest impression over the decades of our love affair with the automobile were simply good, and kept being good for long after our expectations had dropped. What other car has absolutely demolished expectations quite like the Ford Crown Victoria?


This look back doesn’t come out of nowhere. Today marks 15 years since the last Crown Victoria rolled off the assembly line at the St. Thomas assembly plant in Southwold, Ontario. From taxis to commuters to law enforcement, the model was a staple of traffic around the U.S. for decades.


The Crown Victoria package could be found on LTD models in 1980 and 1981.


Ford


It was possible to get the Crown Victoria as a station wagon, too.


Ford


The Crown Victoria name traces back further than the model, first starting as a trim on Fairlane cars in the mid-1950s and resurfacing again to become a trim package on the LTD in the 1980s. Eventually the Crown Victoria became its own model for 1992, and a legend was born. Underpinned by an updated but already aging Panther platform, the Crown Vic was the hearty meat-and-potatoes sedan that excelled in fleets but struggled with the general public as tastes shifted to smaller cars and then to SUVs. Power came from the modular 4.6-liter V-8 backed by a four-speed automatic. Unexciting, but durable and easy to maintain.


Ford


Ford

As it chugged along on fleet sales later in its life, the Crown Victoria was quietly building a reputation that it would only cash in on toward the end of its run. Modern car enthusiasts in search of reliable rear-drive V-8s soon sniffed out the ‘Vic, and it became a cult favorite before jumping to primetime with stunts and appreciation from internet stars like[Cleetus McFarland](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/smithology/smithology-the-cleetus-mcfactor/) , a YouTube personality who built an entire empire hosting circle-track races pitting stars and racers in retired police-spec Crown Victorias against one another and the track in a version of stock-car racing NASCAR hasn’t seen in decades.


Total production was 1.5 million cars, with 1.7 million more dressed up as Mercury Grand Marquis models. The Crown Victoria had a mostly utilitarian life, but somehow its second act has led it to cult stardom. What was once just a cab or a cop car now brings together an array of drivers who might not otherwise have anything else in common besides a durable V-8 sedan that can take a pounding and have a little fun. It was 15 years ago that the last Crown Victoria was built, but they will be forever fresh in our hearts.
